articles.title: Nvidia GB300 is coming to desktop workstations as HP launches the ZGX Fury
articles.text:
Your next desktop PC for the price of a Ferrari? HP ZGX Fury packs in 748GB RAM and Nvidia GB300 — but prices start at $132,000
HP ZGX Fury costs as much as a luxury electric SUV
- HP's latest workstation packs 748GB of memory and Nvidia's GB300 processor
- The ZGX Fury starts at an eye-watering $132,000
- LPDDR5X and HBM3e memory combine to provide 748GB total capacity
HP has introduced an expensive workstation that brings computing hardware previously associated with large-scale AI infrastructure into an office-sized machine.
The ZGX Fury G1n combines Nvidia's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra processor with an enormous memory allocation designed for demanding artificial intelligence workloads.
Its starting price of $132,000 makes it considerably more expensive than conventional professional computers, even before customers consider optional upgrades
HP crams 748GB memory into its expensive workstation
The mobile workstation combines two different memory technologies, LPDDR5X and HBM3e, with 496GB allocated to system memory and another 252GB dedicated to graphics processing.
The LPDDR5X allocation runs at 6,400 MT/s and connects to a 72-core Arm Neoverse V2 Grace CPU, supporting demanding processing workloads.
Meanwhile, the HBM3e memory is integrated into Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra GPU, providing dedicated high-bandwidth capacity for graphics and AI operations.
Customers opting for additional graphics hardware can increase the available video memory to 276GB through selected configurations.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Together, these components provide the advertised 748GB capacity, although customers purchasing additional graphics hardware can increase available video memory to 276GB.
HP also offers configurations featuring discrete Nvidia RTX PRO workstation graphics cards, including the RTX PRO 2000 and RTX PRO 4000.
The memory capacity serves a particular purpose beyond running conventional office applications or demanding professional software.
Developers and researchers working with large language models can use the machine to process substantial workloads without depending entirely on remote computing infrastructure.
HP says the available memory can accommodate local adjustment of language models containing up to 100 billion parameters.
The system can also perform inference using models reaching one trillion parameters through FP4 quantization, although actual performance depends on workload requirements.
Liquid cooling and networking accompany the $132,000 price
Running powerful computing components inside a relatively compact enclosure introduces thermal management requirements that ordinary desktop cooling systems cannot necessarily accommodate.
HP therefore equips the workstation with liquid cooling alongside a 1,600W Titanium-certified power supply.
The device ships with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, making Linux its supplied operating system rather than Microsoft's Windows environment.
This configuration caters to developers and technical professionals who need software environments suitable for demanding computing and AI development.
Networking is another important component, with an Nvidia ConnectX-8 SuperNIC providing two QSFP112 connections rated at 400Gbps.
These connections allow multiple machines to communicate through high-speed networking when organizations need additional computing resources.
The enclosure also supports installation inside a 5U equipment rack, giving organizations another deployment option beyond placing it beneath an office desk.
This flexibility allows organizations to deploy the workstation individually or install multiple units inside equipment racks for larger computing operations.
Getting all these specifications will cost $132,000 for the standard configuration, enough to buy a brand-new 2026 Cadillac Escalade IQL, although not quite a Ferrari.
Customers opting for the RTX PRO 2000 configuration will pay $133,000, while the more powerful RTX PRO 4000 option raises the price to $136,000.
At these prices, the ZGX Fury is unlikely to attract ordinary desktop buyers looking for additional memory or improved everyday computing performance.
Instead, its potential customers are organizations that require substantial local computing resources and can justify spending considerably more than conventional workstation prices.

articles.title: Italy Fines Meta €805 Million Over Facebook's Android Gallery Access Without Explicit Consent
articles.text:
Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for them to post.
The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent.
The company has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately.
Meta plans to appeal and calls the fine "disproportionate", a spokesperson said in a statement reported by Reuters.
The app asks for gallery access via a single permission that covers the whole app and several functions with different purposes, the authority found. A general notice about enabling other features appears first, but it does not make it clear to users that they are also enabling gallery suggestions.
Fully granted, a permission like this lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive, usually on an ongoing basis. Neither the user nor the authority can check which information is actually used.
The authority found a breach of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which puts the EU's ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats a phone as part of a person's private life. Any access to what the phone stores, therefore, requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results.
The authority's order, set out in its press release, requires the company to:
- Within 60 days, ask for consent through a separate, specific request for this feature, and explain clearly what the feature is for, that it accesses the gallery, and how to turn it off.
- Within 60 days, keep the feature off by default, including for people who already granted the permission.
- Within 30 days, report to the authority on the work it has started, and within 90 days, on the measures it has taken.
If the company misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent.
Meta said in a statement quoted in a Reuters report that the feature works only after users give permission on their device, and that they can change that permission at any time in their settings.
The Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti, the Bolzano consumer protection group whose complaint started the investigation, published consumer advice on July 11, 2025. It told users to switch off the gallery suggestion settings in the app and to check what access and permissions the Facebook app has on their phone.
The investigation did not look at whether gallery content was used to train AI models. The company denies any such use. The authority may separately examine a newer feature, launched this year, that allows gallery content to be processed in the cloud.
The company had argued that Ireland's data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules do not provide a one-stop-shop mechanism.
The feature has been available since 2023. The investigation began in July 2025 and included the authority's own technical analysis.
The fine equals about 0.47% of the group's global revenue. In setting it, the authority weighed the large number of people involved, about 20 million Android users in Italy.
It also weighed how long the breach has lasted. The breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the app, and for those who have already granted permission, the authority said.
Other factors were a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation. Changes the company made after the complaint counted in its favor, though the authority judged them late and limited to people who update the app.

articles.title: Cursor Says Stolen Fireworks AI Key Led to Trojanized Claude Code Extension Incident
articles.text:
The compromise of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension on Cursor's extension marketplace was the result of the theft of an access key that was exposed in the wake of a breach targeting Fireworks AI.
"An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said in a Friday update. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them."
The disclosure comes nearly two weeks after a trojanized version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through Cursor Marketplace as a legitimate update, attempting to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems.
According to the artificial intelligence (AI)-powered coding platform, the read-only storage bucket is said to have contained limited coding agent traces from sessions that were not in Privacy Mode. Privacy Mode is a Cursor-specific setting that, if enabled, allows users to opt out of their data being used for training purposes.
These sessions, most of which date back to 2025, were permitted to be used for model training. Among these traces were credentials that had not been edited out, exposing the API credentials of less than 0.01% of customers in the process.
The attacker, Cursor added, used these credentials as a starting point to reach select software-as-a-service (SaaS) tools used by Cursor and then access the following data -
- Select archived non-production Cursor source code repositories, including some containing business contact information
- Limited customer support data and email conversations
- Product usage metrics and contact details
- Summaries of some coding agent conversations
- Some credentials users had sent to the Cursor support team
Cursor said it took steps to deactivate the vendor's key, revoke and rotate credentials, and hunt for signs of deeper access, and contain it after "we identified further access." The company also said it temporarily disabled internal and product services, disrupting access to some Cursor features.
The next phase of the attack took place on October 29, 2026, when the attacker used a stolen credential from the exposed data of its internal system to place trojanized versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve Cursor's extension marketplace.
"At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build," Cursor said. "It was available for approximately 11 hours before we removed it. We took it down, took the extension marketplace offline, and worked with the cloud service provider hosting the attacker's server to take it down."
The company said it notified affected users who installed versions 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the marketplace during the exposure window and helped revoke exposed credentials. It has also moved all inference traffic off Fireworks, deactivated the key issued to it, and cut off its access to all data sets we shared with it.
Furthermore, Cursor emphasized that no additional malicious activity has been detected since November 1, 2026.
There is no evidence that the incident impacted users who had enabled Privacy Mode, customer code repositories, Cursor's own production environment, Cursor app and its official updates, its other apps, or any other extension or plugin downloaded from Cursor Marketplace.
Uber Also Impacted by Fireworks Incident
The development comes as Uber confirmed unknown threat actors stole thousands of drivers' license information after obtaining internal credentials.
"On October 9, 2026, a service provider notified Uber that an unauthorized third-party had compromised the service provider's internal credentials and used them to access Uber's account with the service provider," the company said in a filing with the U.S. state of California. "On October 13, 2026, our investigation determined that the unauthorized party had used the compromised credentials to access Uber data connected to the service provider."
Although the name of the provider was not disclosed, TechCrunch reported that the provider in question is Fireworks AI. Uber has not disclosed how many users were impacted by the breach. Last week, online productivity startup Notion also confirmed its data was stolen in the Fireworks AI hack.

articles.title: This underrated iPhone 18 Pro upgrade has changed my mobile life for the better
articles.text:
The iPhone 18 Pro's C2 modem has transformed my terrible signal — and I'm not the only one who's noticed the benefits
This small iPhone upgrade has changed my life for the better
It's fair to say that the headline-grabbing arrival of the iPhone Duo has made the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max feel a little less shiny than they otherwise might have.
Indeed, upon opening my new iPhone 18 Pro Max and restoring my data from its predecessor, the iPhone 17 Pro Max, it was hard not to feel a little disappointed by the lack of bells and whistles on Apple’s latest flagship.
That’s probably to be expected from a single-generation upgrade — and, to be fair, I don’t usually swap phones after just one year — but there is one feature that’s caught my eye during my time with my iPhone 18 Pro Max, and it’s been a game-changer for my everyday life: Apple’s new C2 modem.
An underrated upgrade
I’ve been using iPhones for around two decades, but since moving to a more remote area in 2021, I have noticed that my mobile signal has been incredibly inconsistent (on some days, it's absolutely awful).
In truth, this spotty signal has been the bane of my digital life, both as a small business owner and a parent — I could be in the same spot on different days of the week and experience completely different levels of coverage. Worse yet, my recent iPhones have had a tendency to display a weak 5G signal when, in fact, there's been no signal at all.
With the iPhone 18 Pro Max, however, I’m seeing drastic improvements in signal strength just about everywhere I go.
Rather than awkwardly trying to fumble through phone tasks using train or café WiFi, I’ve actually been able to use my paid-for data plan consistently, which has made my iPhone 18 Pro Max feel less like a very expensive iPod and more like a piece of cutting-edge computing. And that’s all thanks to the C2 modem.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
What is the C2 modem?
Apple debuted its C1 chip in the iPhone 16e, and the C2 makes its debut in the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo.
The C2 features in every iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo model sold worldwide, but only in iPhone 18 Pro Max models sold outside of the US. If you’re in the US and have Apple's larger Pro model, you’ve got Qualcomm's Snapdragon X80 modem.
Apple hasn't yet disclosed why this is the case, but we suspect it's a result of contractual obligation (we know it's not a technical limitation, since the C2 modem features in all other iPhone 18 Pro Max models, and indeed even in iPhone 18 Pro models sold within the US).
As you'd expect from a numbered hardware upgrade, the C2 modem improves on the C1 in several ways. It adds full mmWave support alongside the C1's existing sub-6GHz 5G capabilities, and consumes less energy than its predecessor.
There are other iPhone 18 Pro-specific advantages, too: “If an iPhone encounters congested data networks, the phone’s [A20 Pro] processor can signal to the modem which traffic is the most time-sensitive and put it ahead of other data transfers,” Apple told Reuters of its C2 modem.
There are dozens of us!
Thankfully, I’m not alone in feeling the benefits of Apple’s C2 modem. Plenty of other iPhone 18 Pro users have found that the addition of this small feature is leading to much better 5G connectivity.
Of course, as this Reddit post mentions, a new modem will only help if you’re in an area covered by 5G in the first place. Luckily for me, my home isn't so remote as to rely on older-generation networks, but that's worth bearing in mind if you live out in the sticks (Apple's hardware wizardry can only work so much magic).
And don't get me wrong: a new 5G modem is hardly the most exciting upgrade on a phone that costs at least $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099, and perhaps it's the least we should expect from Apple when the year-on-year upgrades are so limited elsewhere.
Still, after years of awkwardly lifting my iPhone into the sky in the hope of securing stronger signal — or just simply not using my iPhone at all — this small improvement, combined with improved battery life and the ever-higher performance ceiling of this year’s chip upgrade, has made me appreciate the iPhone 18 Pro Max more than I originally anticipated.
2026 is still very much an ‘iPhone S-year’, though.

articles.title: Cómo cuidar una freidora de aire: 5 trucos para evitar daños y reemplazos prematuros
articles.text:
La freidora de aire permite preparar comidas con menos aceite y en poco tiempo, pero su rendimiento depende de ciertos hábitos de uso y mantenimiento. Una limpieza insuficiente, el uso de utensilios inadecuados o una cesta sobrecargada pueden afectar sus piezas y acortar la vida útil del electrodoméstico.
Para evitar daños y reemplazos antes de tiempo, se debe seguir una rutina antes y después de cada preparación, sumado a respetar las condiciones de uso del aparato.
El fabricante Mouvair sugiere cinco trucos centrados en la limpieza, el cuidado del revestimiento, la capacidad de cocción, el almacenamiento y la elección de recipientes.
Por qué se debe lavar la freidora de aire después de cada uso
La limpieza posterior a cada uso evita que queden restos de grasa y alimentos adheridos en la cesta. Con el paso de las preparaciones, esa acumulación puede generar olores y transferir sabores de una receta a otra.
Un electrodoméstico que se utilizó para cocinar pescado, por ejemplo, puede dejar rastros en preparaciones posteriores si no se higieniza de forma correcta.
Antes de limpiar, es necesario esperar a que la freidora se enfríe y desconectarla de la corriente. La cesta y las piezas removibles pueden lavarse con agua tibia, detergente y una esponja suave.
Qué utensilios ayudan a proteger la cesta de la freidora de aire
Los utensilios de metal pueden rayar el recubrimiento antiadherente de la cesta al retirar o mover los alimentos. Cuando esa superficie se deteriora, los ingredientes tienden a pegarse con mayor facilidad y la limpieza puede requerir más esfuerzo. Las esponjas abrasivas pueden afectar el acabado de la pieza.
Para reducir ese riesgo, es preferible usar pinzas, espátulas y cucharas de madera, silicona u otros materiales blandos. Es clave elegir paños o esponjas no abrasivas para retirar restos de comida. Estas precauciones contribuyen a conservar el revestimiento y evitan que pequeñas marcas se conviertan en daños más extensos.
Por qué no se debe llenar la cesta de la freidora de aire hasta el borde
Una cesta con muchos alimentos dificulta la circulación del aire caliente, que es el sistema de cocción central de este tipo de aparatos. Si las piezas quedan amontonadas, la preparación puede ser desigual: algunas partes se dorarán antes, mientras otras conservarán humedad o requerirán más tiempo.
Respetar la capacidad del fabricante ayuda a obtener resultados más parejos y a no exigir de más al aparato. Cuando hay muchas porciones para cocinar, es preferible dividirlas en tandas. Aunque el proceso demande algunos minutos adicionales, evita tener que repetir la preparación por una cocción incompleta.
Cómo guardar la freidora si no se utilizará durante mucho tiempo
La freidora de aire necesita un lugar seco y protegido cuando no se utilizará durante semanas o meses. Dejarla expuesta sobre una mesada o en un ambiente con humedad puede favorecer la acumulación de polvo y afectar componentes como el cable y el enchufe.
Los fabricantes aconsejan conservar el aparato en su caja original, siempre que sea posible, y ubicarlo en un sitio fresco y seco. Antes de guardarlo, hay que comprobar que la cesta esté completamente limpia y seca. Evitar la humedad y el polvo reduce el riesgo de encontrar residuos adheridos o señales de deterioro al volver a usarla.
Qué moldes utilizar dentro de una freidora de aire sin problemas
Algunas recetas, como galletas, budines, lasañas o preparaciones con salsas, requieren moldes que contengan los ingredientes dentro de la cesta. Para esos casos, deben utilizarse recipientes aptos para altas temperaturas, como los de vidrio tipo pírex u otros materiales resistentes al calor.
El molde debe entrar sin bloquear el paso del aire ni forzar la cesta. Si no se cuenta con un recipiente adecuado, puede utilizarse papel de aluminio con precaución, siempre que no cubra por completo la circulación interna.
Elegir accesorios compatibles con el electrodoméstico evita que los alimentos se adhieran al fondo y reduce el riesgo de dañar el recubrimiento al intentar retirarlos.

articles.title: Subir el rendimiento del PC es posible con este truco gratis y oculto en Windows 11
articles.text:
Windows 11 guarda una función poco conocida capaz de acelerar el ordenador sin gastar dinero en hardware nuevo. Se trata de un conjunto de ajustes y de una tecnología en pruebas que reducen la carga sobre el procesador y la tarjeta gráfica.
La compañía amplía así las herramientas disponibles para mejorar el funcionamiento del equipo. Algunas están a la vista en los menús del sistema; otras permanecen ocultas o todavía se prueban dentro del programa Windows Insider.
Qué es la tecnología APX y cómo mejora el procesador
Microsoft prueba actualmente una función llamada Advanced Performance Extensions, conocida como APX, dentro de la Build 29695 de Windows Insider. Fue desarrollada por Intel para procesadores con arquitectura x86.
APX es una tecnología de Intel que duplica los registros de propósito general del procesador, de 16 a 32, para que el chip trabaje con más datos sin recurrir tanto a la memoria RAM. Las primeras pruebas muestran un 10 % menos de cargas, más de un 20 % menos de almacenamientos y una reducción del 10 % en las instrucciones necesarias.
Al aumentar esos registros, el procesador retiene más información internamente y reduce los viajes hacia la memoria, un proceso que suele ralentizar las tareas. Por tratarse de una función en fase de pruebas, no está disponible todavía para todos los equipos.
Cómo desactivar los efectos visuales en Windows 11
Mientras APX avanza en fase experimental, existe un ajuste ya disponible para cualquier usuario: desactivar las animaciones de la interfaz. Windows 11 construye su diseño sobre Fluent Design, un lenguaje visual con menús translúcidos y transiciones suaves que exige bastante a la tarjeta gráfica.
La propia documentación de Microsoft reconoce que renderizar el material Acrylic, el acabado translúcido de menús y ventanas, supone un esfuerzo considerable para la GPU. En portátiles con varios años de uso o en miniPC con procesadores modestos, ese esfuerzo se nota en la respuesta del sistema y en el consumo de batería.
Para desactivar las animaciones desde la aplicación de Configuración, los pasos son los siguientes:
Pulsar las teclas Windows + I para abrir Configuración. Seleccionar Accesibilidad en el menú de la izquierda. Entrar en Efectos visuales. Desactivar la opción Efectos de animación.
Cómo quitar la transparencia de menús y ventanas
La misma sección de Accesibilidad permite desconectar otro efecto que consume recursos de la GPU: la transparencia. El interruptor también puede localizarse en Personalización > Colores, bajo el nombre Efectos de transparencia.
Al desactivarlo, los menús y las ventanas pierden el acabado translúcido y la carga sobre la tarjeta gráfica disminuye, algo que en equipos con hardware limitado suele traducirse en una navegación más ágil. Transparencia y animaciones son interruptores independientes, de modo que pueden apagarse por separado sin tocar el resto de ajustes del sistema.
El atajo del Panel de Control para ajustar el rendimiento
Windows conserva además una herramienta clásica capaz de desactivar varios efectos de una sola vez. Basta con escribir «Ajustar la apariencia y el rendimiento de Windows» en el buscador de la barra de tareas para acceder a ella.
También puede llegarse por la vía tradicional: abrir el Panel de Control, entrar en Sistema y seguridad, seleccionar Sistema y pulsar en Configuración avanzada del sistema. Desde la pestaña Opciones avanzadas, en el apartado Rendimiento, se accede a Configuración.
Dentro de la pestaña Efectos visuales, la opción Ajustar para obtener el mejor rendimiento desconecta de golpe animaciones, sombras y transiciones. El cambio se aplica a todo el sistema a la vez, aunque modifica el aspecto del escritorio de forma más notoria que si solo se apagara la transparencia.
Revisar las aplicaciones que arrancan con el sistema
Los efectos visuales no son el único freno en equipos antiguos. Los programas que se cargan automáticamente al encender el ordenador restan recursos desde el primer segundo, antes incluso de abrir una ventana.
Para controlarlos, se abre el Administrador de tareas con Ctrl + Shift + Esc y se entra en la pestaña Aplicaciones de inicio, donde aparece el listado completo de programas que arrancan junto con Windows. Ninguno se desinstala al deshabilitarlo: siguen disponibles y pueden reactivarse en cualquier momento desde el mismo menú.
Qué diferencia marca según el tipo de equipo
Microsoft advierte en su documentación de que estos ajustes no suponen una mejora relevante en PC gaming modernos, cuyas tarjetas gráficas absorben sin esfuerzo el coste de renderizar Fluent Design.
La situación cambia en portátiles con varios años de uso o en miniPC de procesador modesto. Ahí, desactivar transparencia y animaciones puede traducirse en una respuesta más ágil del sistema y en una batería que aguanta más tiempo sin cargador, a cambio de un escritorio con un acabado visual más plano.

articles.title: The Samsung S85H is a superb budget OLED TV that’s excellent for gaming and movies — at the right price, it might even be better than the LG B6
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Samsung S85H is a mostly great budget OLED that delivers brilliant picture quality and is fantastic for gaming. Its built-in sound is just average and there are some minor shortcomings, but overall, this is another superb affordable OLED that holds its own against rivals TVs like the LG B6 and TCL QM7L/C7L.
- 
Features Fully stocked for movies, gaming and smart TV.
- 
Picture Quality Excellent colors and contrast, with some minor issues.
- 
Sound Quality Great accuracy and some punch, but bass and soundstage lacking.
- 
Design Razor-thin, lightweight: looks pricier than it is.
- 
Smart TV & Menus Tizen is mostly good, but doesn't beat webOS or Roku.
- 
Gaming Every feature you need and fantastic performance.
- 
Value Rival LG B6 is cheaper, but still offers superb bang-for-your-buck.
Reasons to buy
- + Great picture quality
- + Brilliant for gaming
- + Affordable for OLED
Reasons to avoid
- - No Dolby Vision
- - Average sound
- - Samsung S90H is a big upgrade
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Samsung S85H review: Two-minute review
The Samsung S85H is great entry-level OLED TV that can compete with the best TVs of 2026. It offers a near-full feature set, with brilliant performance at a competitive price. While its closest rival, the LG B6, is cheaper at the moment, and arguably the better buy — as I found when I compared it and the S85H side-by-side — this is still a very capable TV.
The S85H’s picture quality is excellent overall. It delivers punchy, vibrant colors, strong contrast, crisp, realistic textures and good motion handling. It does have a reflective screen, an issue the step-up Samsung S90H doesn’t suffer from, and there are sometimes black-crush issues in darker scenes, but the S85H’s picture is competitive with the best OLED TVs.
Sound quality in the S85H is a mixed bag. It has great accuracy, and at times punchy bass, but generally its limited two-channel speaker system can only do so much. Sound feels contained to the back of the screen, and while there is some extension beyond the TV’s frame, it doesn’t offer what one of the best soundbars could. It’s fine for day-to-day viewing, but you’ll want a soundbar if you’re after a more cinematic experience.
For gaming, the S85H is a fantastic budget-OLED option. It has a suite full of features up there with the best gaming TVs — 4K 120Hz, FreeSync and G-Sync, HDR10+ gaming and ALLM — as well as ultra-low input lag and four HDMI 2.1 ports. Its performance is responsive and smooth, and it serves as a superb gaming TV.
The S85H is good value for money. The 55-inch model I tested costs $999 / £999 / AU$1,999, putting it in the more affordable OLED bracket. While its nearest rival, the LG B6, is cheaper ($799 / £999 / AU$1,699 for the 55-inch), making it the better-value buy, the S85H still offers brilliant performance and features for the price, and that price is only going to get cheaper.
Samsung S85H review: Prices & release date
- Release date: June 2026
- 48-inch: $799 / £899 / AU$1,399
- 55-inch: $999 / £999 / AU$1,999
- 65-inch: $1,199 / £1,399 / AU$2,299
- 77-inch: $1,799 / £1,999 / AU$3,299
- 83-inch: $2,799 / £2,699 / AU$4,999
The Samsung S85H is the entry-level model in Samsung’s 2026 OLED TV lineup, sitting below the mid-range S90H and flagship S95H/S99H. It’s available in sizes 48-83-inch, with the 55-inch model I tested launching for $1,499 / £1,399 / AU$2,499 in May-June 2026 (depending on region).
Since its release, the S85H’s prices have dropped across all sizes and in all regions. The 55-inch is now available (November 2026) for around $999 / £999 / AU$1,899, though you can find it for less at some retailers in some regions. The rival LG B6 55-inch is cheaper at the moment in the US and Australia, costing $799 / £999 / AU$1,699, but it’s likely that the ‘cheaper’ title will change hands a few times during these TV’s life cycles.

Samsung S85H review: Features
- WOLED panel
- NQ4 AI Gen 2 Processor
- Tizen smart TV platform and Vision AI
The S85H uses a WOLED panel, the same one as in the rival LG B6 and the same as the step-up S90H, though some sizes are reported to have QD-OLED. The S90H benefits from the upgraded NQ4 AI Gen 3 Processor, which allows for higher brightness and better color performance, while the S85H has the older NQ4 AI Gen 2 Processor built in. The Gen 2 is no slouch, though, and supports picture features such as 4K AI Upscaling and Real Depth Enhancer Pro.
The S85H supports HDR10+, including the new HDR10+ Advanced, HDR10 and HLG HDR formats, but as usual with Samsung TVs, there’s no support for Dolby Vision.
For audio, the S85H has a 2-channel, 20W speaker system with support for Dolby Atmos. A number of AI sound features are included too, such as AI Sound Pro, as well as Object Tracking Sound (OTS) Lite. Q-Symphony, where the TV’s speakers can be used in conjunction with a supported Samsung soundbar, is also featured.
The S85H supports 4K 120Hz, full VRR including AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync, ALLM and HDR10+ gaming, which works across all of the S85H’s four HDMI 2.1 ports. There’s also a Game Hub, where cloud gaming apps are housed.
Tizen serves as the S85H’s smart TV platform, supporting all major streaming apps such as Netflix and Disney Plus. Tizen also features the Vision AI companion, which uses multiple AI agents to make content and even lifestyle recommendations you may ask such as recommended places for dinner.
- Features score: 5 / 5
Samsung S85H review: Picture quality
- Great color reproduction
- Strong contrast
- Somewhat reflective screen
As the S85H uses a standard WOLED panel, its brightness doesn’t match that of step-up OLEDs like the S90H or LG C6. In my testing it clocked a peak HDR brightness (on a 10% window pattern) of 833 nits and 854 nits in Filmmaker Mode and Standard respectively. Those scores put it in line with the rival LG B6E (which hit 808 nits and 727 nits in the same respective modes), but are much lower than those achieved by the step-up S90H, which measured 1,689 and 1677 in the same two modes.
As for fullscreen brightness, the S85H hit just over 150 nits in both Filmmaker and Standard, which is about right for WOLED, but it’s still a significant drop compared to rival mini-LEDs such as the TCL QM7L/C7L, which hit over 600 nits. This means the S85H can struggle in bright rooms, and without an effective anti-glare coating, dark scenes can be hard to watch in brighter conditions, so this TV is best suited to viewing in ambient or dark conditions. Samsung’s step-up S90H OLED, on the other hand, easily handles bright rooms.
Starting with SDR content, the S85H does a good job of upscaling textures. Watching various programs on Samsung TV Plus, textures did look cleaner and sharpened than you’d get on some standard LED and mini-LED TVs, and with bolder colors. While the step-up S90H did a better job with upscaling, the S85H’s was still impressive nonetheless.
Switching to 4K HDR content, the S85H delivers excellent colors. Watching Elemental on Disney Plus in HDR10+, the bold oranges of the fire people and blues of the water people pop throughout the movie, even in the slightly dimmer Filmmaker Mode. Putting the S85H in Movie mode adds more brightness and a bit more color depth which works well for the animation. As Ember runs across multi-colored minerals, colors have a nice shine to them, showing the S85H’s punchy HDR highlights.
Watching a live-action movie, The Sound of Music, the S85H shows it can render realistic-looking colors too. The green fields and blue skies of Austria look wonderfully natural whenever they’re on screen, and the S85H shows true-to-life skin tones in the people as well.
Measuring the S85H’s HDR color-gamut coverage, it registered 97.9% of the UHDA-P3 and 73.4% of the BT.2020 color spaces. These numbers are about right for a WOLED TV, but are starting to fall behind those of more premium OLEDs and RGB mini-LED TVs. Still the S85H’s colors were great overall.
The S85H also demonstrates strong contrast. In The Batman, which includes lots of scenes with lights cutting through the dark environments, such as in the Batcave and in aerial shots of Gotham, the S85H shows an excellent balance between these light and dark tones to create an authentic image. The same is true in Project Hail Mary, with both shots of space and scenes inside the ship showing the S85H’s powerful contrast and deep black levels.
Shadow detail is also great, with details and textures legible in challenging dark scenes, such as frames on the wall of Mayor Mitchell’s house in The Batman. I did notice during some particularly dark shots that the S85H was prone to some black crush, even in pitch-black viewing conditions. For the most part however, its contrast was impressive.
The S85H also demonstrated crisp textures in nearly every scene I watched, with people in particular looking true-to-life. This 3D-like level of detail was one of the S85H’s strengths over the LG B6E when I tested the two side-by-side, showcasing the effectiveness of the Real Depth Enhancer feature.
Finally, the S85H demonstrated very good motion for both sports and movies, although some setup is required. I found setting blur reduction to 3 and judder reduction between 3-5 (depending on the content and how fluid you want your picture) was the most effective. There were still some motion artefacts when watching a soccer match on Prime Video, with some blurring of textures in some shots, but the S85H was mostly effective.
- Picture quality score: 4.5 / 5
Samsung S85H review: Sound quality
- Great accuracy thanks to OTS Lite system
- Very good detail
- Soundstage and bass can be narrow
The S85H’s two-channel, 20W speaker system isn’t strong enough to allow you to skimp on a soundbar if you want powerful and immersive sound for action-heavy movies and shows, and doesn’t match up to step-up TVs, but is mostly fine for day-to-day viewing and some movies.
Watching the Batmobile scene from The Batman, the S85H’s strength lay in the accuracy of sound, showing how effective the OTS Lite system was. As the Batmobile swerved through traffic, screeching tires and car horns were mapped with real accuracy between the sound and action on the screen.
Impacts also generated some nice punch. As the Batmobile clatters through a barricade, the sound of scraping metal had some weight to it, and as the Batmobile’s engine revved, there was some punchy bass. However, when I pushed the volume, the bass did seem to fizzle out, and high-end sound could be a little harsh.
While I did hear some extension of sound from the frame of the screen, particularly during the aforementioned swerving manoeuvres, the sound felt contained to the rear of the screen, making it feel like the viewing experience was lacking some depth. Speech was mostly clear throughout, but could get lost at times. Again, you want a cinematic experience, I’d hook up a soundbar.
- Sound quality: 3.5 / 5
Samsung S85H review: Design
- Thin frame
- Two-position option for feet (55-inch)
- Lightweight build
The most striking thing visually about the S85H is how thin it is compared to rival TVs in this price range. It has a sleek, metal frame and a razor-thin depth that suggest a more premium price. Even its rear panel is fairly trim, with only a small bump to accommodate the connection ports.
For the 55-inch model I tested, two plastic feet were supplied which, while they felt a little cheap, were very easy to install. You can choose between two positions for the feet, narrow and wide, with the latter being very useful if you have a soundbar. The TV is also very light for a 55-inch model, but still felt sturdy when placed on a TV stand.
The S85H comes with Samsung’s SolarCell remote, which offers solar and USB-C charging. Its small size means it could get lost quite easily, but it feels light in the hand, and offers all the usual options (streaming app shortcuts, settings, power and volume).
- Design score: 4.5 / 5
Samsung S85H review: Smart TV & menus
- Tizen One UI platform
- Good number of picture settings
- Some frustrations with home screen
Samsung’s own Tizen serves as the smart TV platform for the S85H, and with it come a host of AI features via the Vision AI companion, which uses AI agents to help with content recommendation, lifestyle advice, and more general questions you might ask of a smart assistant (how long is a day on Jupiter was one of the example prompts). There are also a host of AI Picture and sound features via the AI Mode settings (found under the Advanced Features menu), such as AI Soccer Mode and Adaptive Sound Pro.
Tizen’s main three hubs on the main screen — For You, Live, and Game and Apps — host recommended content, live TV, gaming content and a general apps page respectively. These pages are generally laid out well, but do have banner ads that take up about a third of the page. I also found Samsung TV Plus autoplays on the For You page and can sometimes take over the page if left idle, which can be frustrating.
You can choose from a good number of picture settings, all housed in logical places within the settings menu. Some of these settings, such as Auto HDR Remastering for SDR content, can be effective. Sound settings are a bit more limited, and I’d have liked more than two sound mode options. Tizen is a solid interface overall, but doesn’t quite match up to LG’s webOS or Roku for ease-of-use.
- Smart TV and menus score: 4 / 5
Samsung S85H review: Gaming
- Four HDMI 2.1 ports
- Ultra-low 9.2ms input lag time
- Game hub
The S85H is an excellent choice for gaming. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, perfect for multiple consoles, and all of these support 4K 120Hz, full VRR including FreeSync and G-Sync, ALLM and HDR10+ gaming. The featured Game Hub is a useful home for all things gaming, and offers quick access to a connected console and cloud gaming apps.
The S85H’s input lag registered 9.2ms at 4K 60Hz and 4.5ms at 1080p 120Hz, the latter of which is one of the lowest scores I’ve seen. This translates into actual gaming too. Playing Battlefield V, motion felt incredibly smooth with razor-sharp response times — extremely useful when faced with tons of enemies.
Picture-wise, the S85H’s brilliant quality is great for gaming. The colors of autumnal trees during one mission really popped on screen, while textures were very crisp, and, during night-time missions, black tones were deep and contrast was strong.
- Gaming score: 5 / 5
Samsung S85H review: Value
- Great value for money
- Brilliant performance and features
- Rival B6 is cheaper in most places
The 55-inch S85H I tested currently costs $999 / £999 / AU$1,999, which is very good for a budget OLED. Considering the features and performance it delivers, it’s great value for money overall.
Right now, its major rival, the LG B6, is cheaper in most places. A 55-inch LG B6 (or in some cases LG B6E, which isn’t markedly different from the standard B6) costs around $799 / £999 / AU$1,699. The B6 offers near-identical features and performance, so right now it’s the better deal.
The Samsung S90H is a notable step-up over the S85H, offering higher brightness, better picture quality and an anti-reflection screen for bright-room viewing. The 55-inch model costs $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,999, so if you’re in the UK and US and can stretch your budget, it’s worth the upgrade. Still, the S85H is good value overall, and I expect its prices will drop and fall more in line with those of the B6 as time goes on.
- Value score: 4.5 / 5
Should you buy the Samsung S85H?
Buy it if...
You want OLED at a more affordable price
If you're looking for an OLED TV but don't want to fork out the big bucks, the S85H is a perfect gateway into the tech. 
You want great picture quality 
The S85H thrives with colorful movies, but also presents strong contrast and crisp textures that highlight what's to love about OLED
You want a gaming TV
Fully kitted out with four HDMI 2.1 ports and every feature you could need and the performance to go with it, the S85H is perfect for gaming. 
Don't buy it if...
You need Dolby Vision
There's no support for Dolby Vision HDR, which is used on a lot of 4K Blu-rays and streaming services. This is the case with all Samsung TVs. 
You want the best sound
The S85H's built-in sound is solid enough for day-to-day viewing, but if you want a more cinematic experience, you'll need a soundbar. 
You can stretch your budget to the Samsung S90H
In some sizes, the step-up Samsung S90H is only a little pricier and its big upgrade over the S85H, with an anti-glare screen and higher brightness. 
Also Consider
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Samsung S85H | LG B6 | Samsung S90H | TCL QM7L/C7L | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price (55-inch) (current) | $999 / £999 / AU$1,999 | $799 / £899 / AU$1,699 | $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2995 | $699 / £849 / AU$1,395 | 
| Screen type | OLED | OLED | OLED | SQD mini-LED | 
| Refresh rate | 120Hz | 120Hz | 165Hz | 144Hz | 
| HDR support | Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG | Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG | HDR10+, HDR10, HLG | Dolby Vision, HDR10+. HDR10, HLG | 
| Smart TV | Tizen | webOS 26 | Tizen | Google TV | 
| HDMI ports | 4x HDMI 2.1 | 4x HDMI 2.1 | 4 x HDMI 2.1 | 4 (2 x HDMI 2.1) | 
LG B6
The LG B6 is the S85H's closest rival and offers similar performance and features, but for slightly cheaper. The B6 has richer colors and Dolby Vision, while the S85H has crisper textures. Both deliver strong contrast as well, and are full kitted out for gaming. This comes down to whichever model is cheaper. 
Read our full LG B6 review
Samsung S90H
The step-up model from the S85H, the S90H is pricier, but it has an effective anti-glare screen perfect for bright rooms, better picture quality and a better processor. The S90H is worth the investment if you can stretch your budget. 
Read our Samsung S90H review
TCL QM7L/C7L
The TCL QM7L (US)/C7L (UK/Aus) is the brand's mid-range SDQ mini-LED. While the S85H delivers better contrast and textures,  the QM7L/C7L is much brighter and offers competitive gaming features and performance for a similar price. Pick the QM7L/C7L if you have a brighter room. 
Read our TCL QM7L review and TCL C7L review
How I tested the Samsung S85H
- Tested over a couple of weeks
- Testing using SDR and HDR sources in varying lighting conditions
- Measurements taken using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software
I first started my testing of the Samsung S85H with casual viewing to assess which picture mode was best, landing on Filmmaker and Movie modes for movies and TV and Standard for sports and broadcast TV.
I then tested the S85H using reference 4K Blu-ray, analyzing its color, contrast, textures and detail and motion, while also using SDR sports and daytime TV to analyze its upscaling capabilities.
Once these tests were complete, I took measurements using a Murido Six G 8K test pattern generator, a Jeti Spectral 15VA spectroradiometer profiled with the a Klein K-10A colorimeter, and recorded the measurements using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software.
I tested the S85H's brightness, measuring on a white window pattern in sizes 1-100%, with a focus on 10% peak and 100% fullscreen brightness, in both SDR and HDR.
I then measured its color and grayscale accuracy in SDR using Delta-E averages (the margin for error between the test pattern signal and what's displayed on screen).
Next was HDR color gamut coverage, where I sued the UHDA-P3 (the color space used for 4K Blu-ray and digital cinema releases) and BT.2020 (becoming more commonly used) color spaces.
I also measured the S85H's HDR EOTF, using 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000 nits targets, which shows the TV's accuracy between light and dark tones. I also measured its Spectral Power Distribution, which measures its color performance.
Finally, I measured its input lag in both 4K 60Hz and 1080p 120Hz using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMI Input Lag Tester.
Read our in-depth overview of how we test TVs at TechRadar.
- First reviewed: November 2026

When not writing about the latest TV tech, James can be found gaming, reading, watching rugby or coming up with another idea for a novel.

articles.title: Ver España vs Inglaterra en Fútbol Libre o Roja Directa llena el celular de publicidad invasiva y virus
articles.text:
Buscar una transmisión de un partido de la UEFA Nations League, como España vs Inglaterra, en páginas piratas puede tener consecuencias que van más allá de los cortes de señal. Las páginas que prometen ver fútbol gratis pueden redirigir el celular a publicidad invasiva, descargas de virus o aplicaciones maliciosas.
Plataformas como Fútbol Libre o Roja Directa suelen ser buscadas para ver partidos gratis. Estas opciones son peligrosas porque exigen instalar una aplicación, descargar un archivo, aceptar permisos o pulsar repetidamente anuncios para acceder al contenido, según advierte el Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad de España (Incibe).
Por qué los anuncios pueden convertirse en una puerta de entrada a virus
La publicidad invasiva no siempre se limita a abrir una ventana adicional. Algunos avisos imitan botones de reproducción, alertas del sistema o mensajes que anuncian un supuesto virus en el teléfono.
El objetivo puede ser que el usuario descargue una aplicación, complete un formulario o acceda a otra web que recopile información personal.
En ocasiones, el navegador abre varias pestañas de forma automática o muestra anuncios incluso después de cerrar la página original. Esto puede ocurrir si se aceptaron notificaciones de un sitio desconocido o si se instaló una aplicación con funciones publicitarias ocultas.
Qué pasa si se descarga una app pirata para ver partidos sin costo
Una aplicación descargada fuera de Google Play o App Store puede ocultar funciones distintas a las que promete. Puede mostrar publicidad, redirigir el tráfico a otras páginas o recopilar datos del dispositivo.
Incibe advierte que las aplicaciones maliciosas pueden exponer datos personales y facilitar actividades fraudulentas. Antes de instalar cualquier programa, conviene comprobar quién lo desarrolla, consultar valoraciones de otros usuarios y revisar si solicita permisos que no guardan relación con su función.
Se debe considerar que una app para reproducir video no debería necesitar acceso a los contactos, los SMS o la ubicación precisa.
Cómo un virus descargado puede secuestrar datos del dispositivo
Entre las amenazas está el ransomware, un tipo de programa malicioso que bloquea archivos o impide el acceso al dispositivo y después exige un pago. Una persona puede descubrir el problema cuando intenta abrir las fotos, documentos o copias almacenadas en el teléfono y aparece un mensaje que reclama dinero para recuperarlos.
Pagar no garantiza que los archivos vuelvan a estar disponibles. Por eso, las copias de seguridad resultan una medida de protección útil. Los respaldos en servicios de almacenamiento en la nube o en dispositivos externos permiten recuperar información si el celular sufre una infección, un robo o un desperfecto.
De qué forma un ciberdelincuente puede robar contraseñas
No todos los robos de contraseñas comienzan con un mensaje fraudulento. Algunas apps incluyen un keylogger, una herramienta capaz de registrar las pulsaciones que realiza el usuario en la pantalla. De ese modo, podría capturar contraseñas, códigos de acceso y datos introducidos en aplicaciones bancarias o redes sociales.
El peligro crece cuando la app pide permisos de accesibilidad o la posibilidad de superponerse sobre otras aplicaciones. Esas autorizaciones pueden permitir que un programa observe la actividad en pantalla o muestre formularios falsos sobre servicios legítimos.
Si una aplicación instalada para ver fútbol gratis solicita accesos de ese tipo, lo más prudente es denegar el permiso y considerar su desinstalación.
Qué sucede si una app pirata recopila mensajes de texto
Si una aplicación maliciosa obtiene permiso para leer los SMS, podría ver códigos de verificación enviados por bancos, billeteras virtuales o redes sociales.
La revisión de permisos debe hacerse de forma periódica. Hay que retirar el acceso a los SMS, la cámara, el micrófono, los contactos o la ubicación cuando no resulte necesario. Actualizar el sistema operativo, usar una solución de seguridad confiable y descargar apps solo desde tiendas oficiales ayuda a limitar estos riesgos.

articles.title: Publicar un juego en Steam demora hasta tres semanas y los desarrolladores culpan a la IA
articles.text:
Varios estudios independientes esperaron entre dos y tres semanas la aprobación de sus juegos en Steam, la tienda de videojuegos para computadoras de Valve, cuando el plazo habitual es de tres a cinco días. Los desarrolladores sospechan que una avalancha de títulos creados con IA saturó la revisión. Valve reconoció la demora, pero no mencionó esa causa.
El 3 de noviembre, Valve publicó un comunicado para desarrolladores en el que admite “un aumento significativo” de solicitudes de revisión de páginas de tienda y de versiones de juegos en los últimos meses. Según el reportaje de Kotaku, el proceso toma ahora hasta 12 días hábiles.
La empresa explica que la mayor parte del tiempo se va en revisar de nuevo los juegos que presentan problemas al enviarse. Valve afirmó que ajusta sus procesos internos para absorber la carga y que sumará puntos a la lista de verificación previa al lanzamiento, con el fin de reducir los envíos que debe devolver.
Kotaku señala que el comunicado no menciona la inteligencia artificial generativa. La guía oficial de Valve sigue recomendando enviar la página a revisión al menos siete días hábiles antes de la fecha de salida, un margen que varios estudios dicen haber superado sin éxito.
Cómo fue el proceso de espera de estudios durante semanas
Entre los casos que recoge Kotaku, Ashen Legacy se envió el 15 de octubre y recibió la aprobación el 1 de noviembre, cinco días antes de su salida prevista. Caravarn Carnage: Fruity Road pasó la revisión el 1 de noviembre tras enviarse el 16 de octubre. Lacey’s Flash Games salió cuatro días tarde, en Halloween.
Wheel Make It llegó a su público con tres semanas de retraso, según Kotaku. Su estudio contó en redes que el juego fue rechazado en la primera revisión porque los revisores no entendieron cómo activar el modo cooperativo local, que se juega compartiendo un teclado.
El equipo de Cubic Earth, que preparaba su debut en acceso anticipado, dijo a Kotaku que su juego quedó sin fecha de lanzamiento. También afirmó que el tráfico orgánico hacia su página en Steam “se desplomó por completo”, y que los jugadores reclamaron explicaciones por el retraso.
El estudio de nueve personas que sigue esperando
Alfred Kamon, director de Studio Daimon, con sede en Italia, envió Food Devils a revisión el 12 de octubre. Según relató a Kotaku, siguió el consejo de Valve y abrió un ticket de soporte el 24 de octubre. El 26, Valve planteó una objeción por contenido sexual, y él respondió de inmediato.
Siete días después seguía sin respuesta. Kamon dijo que en ocasiones anteriores esos problemas se resolvían en dos o tres días. Sin la aprobación final, tampoco puede entregar claves completas del juego a quienes lo reseñan. Kotaku vio los mensajes entre el estudio y Valve.
El estudio tiene nueve personas y trabajó cuatro años en el juego. Kamon explicó que necesita los ingresos antes de fin de año y que Steam paga con un mes de retraso, por lo que no puede postergar el lanzamiento a diciembre. “Cuéntennos que puede tardar semanas”, pidió, en vez de prometer tres a cinco días.
La sospecha sobre la IA y la postura de Valve
Los desarrolladores apuntan a las cifras. Según Kotaku, hasta mediados de octubre se habían lanzado en Steam más juegos en 2026 que en todo 2025. En octubre salieron cerca de 4.000 títulos, y casi la mitad declaró algún uso de IA generativa, de acuerdo con un informe y un análisis en Reddit que el medio cita.
Kotaku aclara que, sin una explicación más precisa de Valve, nadie puede probar que la IA explique la demora. La compañía sí reconoció antes un problema con contenido de baja calidad, después de que más de 8.000 demos inundaran el evento Steam Next Fest en octubre.
Esa vez, Valve dijo que no quiere ser “guardián” que decida qué herramientas usan los desarrolladores. Marc Wilkinson, de Valve, afirmó: “Somos plenamente conscientes de la situación y un número significativo de personas está pensando cómo resolver este problema”.
Kamon pidió que Valve sea transparente sobre cuánto tardará la revisión y que su juego gane visibilidad en Steam para compensar el retraso. Hasta la publicación del reportaje de Kotaku, Food Devils seguía sin aprobación.

articles.title: The iconic Herman Miller Aeron office chair gets a $482 discount in the Black Friday sale
articles.text:
The iconic Herman Miller Aeron office chair gets a $482 discount in the Black Friday sale
It’s an office icon with premium materials and a 12-year warranty, and now the Herman Miller Aeron is 25% cheaper
The Herman Miller Aeron just got a little cheaper - thanks to the Black Friday sale, this famous office chair is currently available at a starting price of $1,331.25, which is a saving of $443.75 on its usual price of $1,775.
That’s still a huge amount of money, but it’s a premium chair designed for years of daily use - and the Aeron has a reputation for exceptional build quality and ergonomic engineering that few office chairs can match.
Today’s best Herman Miller Aeron Black Friday deal
The Aeron is available directly from Herman Miller, with a wide range of specification options.
So while this deal may start at $1,331.25, that’s for a basic model without adjustable armrests, advanced back support, or tilting.
The Aeron is available in ten different finishes and three sizes, with a variety of lumbar support options, and with different arm and caster variations. The good news is that everything is 25% off, so you’ll save a solid chunk of cash no matter what configuration you choose.
Why we recommend the Herman Miller Aeron
The Aeron’s most distinctive feature is its 8Z Pellicle suspension material, which replaces conventional foam cushioning with a breathable mesh seat and backrest. It’s got eight tension zones that effectively distribute weight evenly across the chair alongside a PostureFit SL system that delivers targeted support for your lumbar region.
We reviewed the closely related Aeron Gaming Chair and were particularly impressed by its impeccable build quality and premium adjustment features - and the fact that it arrived fully assembled, with no building required.
Our reviewer found it supermely comfortable, though they noted that the lack of a headrest and a slightly limited array of armrest options were minor drawbacks.
Read our full Herman Miller Aeron Gaming Chair review here.
Price context and historical value
Black Friday prices start at $1,331.25 and rise to more than $2,000 if you configure with Aeron with its full array of adjustment options. So, no matter how you spec up this chair, it’s a significant investment even with the current 25% discount.
However, remember that Herman Miller’s chair isn’t competing with ordinary budget or mid-range office or gaming chairs. It’s got world-class build quality and design, specialist suspension material, a 12-year warranty, and it arrives fully assembled.
It’s a long-term purchase - almost an investment - rather than something you may have to replace after a couple of years.
If you spend most of your day sitting and want to prioritise design quality and comfort, then the Black Friday discount makes this expensive unit a little easier to justify.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Herman Miller Aeron if… you want exceptional build quality, breathable suspension seating and carefully engineered ergonomic support. It’s particularly appealing if you’re investing in a long-term office setup.
❌ Skip the Herman Miller Aeron if… you want a headrest, plush cushioning or a more relaxed seating position. Its distinctive ergonomic design won’t suit everyone, and even discounted, it’s considerably more expensive than most alternatives.

articles.title: Con descargas falsas están engañando a fans de GTA 6 para robar sus datos y dinero
articles.text:
El lanzamiento de GTA VI, previsto para el 19 de noviembre, se convirtió en el blanco de una ola de estafas digitales que buscan robar contraseñas, instalar programas maliciosos y obtener pagos en criptomonedas.
Rockstar Games no anunció ninguna beta pública, versión para computadora, acceso anticipado ni adaptación móvil del título, por lo que cualquier oferta que prometa jugarlo antes de su estreno o en una plataforma no confirmada debe tomarse como una señal de alerta.
Qué prometen las estafas más frecuentes de GTA 6
Un estudio de la compañía de ciberseguridad Netcraft, que analizó dominios registrados entre el 1 de julio y el 27 de octubre de 2026, identificó cuatro categorías de engaño: sitios que explotan la notoriedad del filtrador “CyberLeek”, plataformas de supuesto acceso anticipado, portales con versiones móviles inexistentes y páginas de sorteos falsos.
Las estafas relacionadas con GTA VI consisten, en esencia, en páginas y mensajes que ofrecen betas, descargas filtradas o accesos VIP inexistentes para robar credenciales, instalar malware o cobrar dinero en criptomonedas antes de que el juego esté disponible de forma oficial.
Un informe de la firma ESET amplió el panorama con una tabla de riesgos que incluye phishing de credenciales, betas falsas, estafas con criptomonedas, tiendas clonadas y distribución directa de malware.
Las filtraciones y los archivos maliciosos
El 18 de agosto, una cuenta identificada como CyberLeek comenzó a difundir material que presentaba como filtrado de GTA VI, incluidos videos de gameplay y un supuesto mapa de Leonida. Rockstar calificó la publicación de “desgarradora” y emprendió acciones legales.
La repercusión disparó el registro de 121 dominios con el término “cyberleek”, de los cuales cien se crearon solo en agosto. No todos eran fraudulentos, pero varios distribuían versiones falsas del juego.
Uno de los casos fue el dominio gta6cyberleek[.]com, que simulaba ser un portal de Rockstar y ofrecía un archivo llamado GTAVI.exe, detectado como troyano por 34 de los 68 motores de seguridad de VirusTotal. Otro sitio, cyberleek[.]click, exigía 100 dólares en criptomonedas para desbloquear un supuesto lanzador.
Investigadores de Malwarebytes hallaron además páginas que imitaban la promoción oficial del adelanto de gameplay difundido en Netflix y ofrecían un instalador de apenas 1,1 MB que en realidad contenía Vidar, un infostealer capaz de robar contraseñas guardadas en 19 navegadores distintos.
Otra campaña, documentada por Huntress, distribuyó imágenes ISO de más de 100 GB rellenas con datos basura para simular el peso de un juego real. Dentro escondían los troyanos njRAT y DCRat, el infostealer Mercurial Grabber y el malware destructivo Chaos, que cifraba o sobrescribía archivos sin ofrecer forma de recuperarlos.
Tiendas falsas y pagos exigidos en criptomonedas
Pese a que Rockstar confirmó el juego únicamente para PlayStation 5 y Xbox Series X|S, el sitio gta6[.]exposed comercializaba una supuesta versión para computadora por 199 dólares en criptomonedas.
Otra estafa documentada por Malwarebytes ofrecía acceso anticipado exclusivo por 250 dólares, con pagos aceptados solo en bitcoin, USDT o ethereum, y un proceso con códigos QR que simulaba una compra real sin que existiera entrega alguna.
Las versiones móviles también se usan como señuelo: existen archivos APK falsos y formularios de “verificación humana” que piden datos personales, pese a que no hay anuncio oficial de GTA VI para Android o iOS.
Cómo evitar estas estafas
Estas son las recomendaciones más importantes a tener en cuenta:
- Comprar solo en tiendas oficiales como PlayStation Store, Microsoft Store o Rockstar Games Store.
- Desconfiar de precios demasiado bajos.
- Investigar la reputación de cualquier tienda desconocida.
- Usar medios de pago con protección al comprador.
- Comparar cada oferta con lo que Rockstar confirmó oficialmente.
- Mantener actualizado el software de seguridad, y actuar rápido ante cualquier sospecha, cambiando contraseñas y cerrando sesiones activas.
La precarga digital, habilitada desde el 10 de noviembre, puede requerir hasta 212 GB según el dispositivo, pero no permite jugar antes del estreno.

articles.title: ‘These aren’t just any earbuds, they’re FlyBuds’: Tribit’s super-cheap buds offer great audio for the money, but this one disappointing issue means I can’t recommend them
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Tribit FlyBuds C3 are a good set of wireless earbuds, with impressive sound quality for the money, strong EQ options, and a comfortable fit. However, their underwhelming battery life and plasticky build slightly hold them back. And while they’re temptingly cheap, their limited ANC is the one thing that stops me from recommending them over similarly priced rivals.
Reasons to buy
- + Good sound quality with powerful bass
- + Highly customizable EQ
- + Compact, comfortable design
Reasons to avoid
- - ANC is light touch
- - Underwhelming battery life
- - Plasticky build
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Tribit FlyBuds C3 review
These aren’t just any earbuds, they’re FlyBuds. And the new Tribit FlyBuds 3 look mighty impressive at a glance, especially when you consider their temptingly low price tag.
The Tribit FlyBuds 3 bring active noise cancellation, highly customizable EQ, and a six-microphone system for 'clear' voice calls. Sounds pretty good for $39.99 / £49.99 (about AU$60), right? But just how good are the FlyBuds C3? I’ve been using them for a couple of weeks now, and this is my verdict.
First up, let’s talk about features. The Tribit FlyBuds C3 offer a lot of the functionality you’d expect from the best wireless earbuds.
Perhaps the main thing is ANC, which has five levels of strength, and can apparently block sounds “up to 45dB”. I have to say, though, that ANC on the FlyBuds C3 is disappointing. On walks, the sounds of nearby chatter and vehicles passing by were dulled, but still pretty audible. And when working in the office, the noise of typing was still pretty clear, even with my music at about 70% volume.
Again, the ANC here will certainly dull your surroundings, but it won’t block them out entirely. With that said, there is a very effective ambient mode that helps you stay aware of your environment when listening to tunes or taking phone calls on the go.
Most of the other features here did impress me, though. You get pretty detailed EQ options, with a number of presets for specific genres and use cases, as well as a full 10-band equalizer if you’re looking for more granular control. In addition, there’s a low-latency game mode, multi-point connectivity, and a hearing protection option.
Something else I appreciated about the FlyBuds C3 was their inclusion of customizable touch controls. By disabling single touch commands, and mapping playback controls to double taps (as well as ANC alterations to press and hold), I was able to avoid accidentally triggering unwanted button presses. You can map specific controls to each individual bud too, which is a great touch.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
I also found the mic quality here to be plenty good enough. When taking phone calls and making a recording, I found that my speech was replicated accurately — I didn’t have to put up with the almost ‘underwater’ quality that some cheap models can apply. I picked up a bit of sibilance, and the microphones’ ability to carve out background noise was pretty limited, but in my view the call quality here is adequate for the price.
There are a few areas that could be improved, though. The X-3D spatial mode just makes music sound louder and less refined, there’s no wear detection or higher-res audio codec support, and the battery life here is surprisingly average.
Yes, you get just five hours from the buds with ANC active and seven hours without noise cancelling on, with up to 35 hours of playtime available with the case (with ANC off). A lot of Tribit’s budget audio tech goes big on battery, so I was expecting more here — that five hours with ANC on is especially weak when you consider you’ll need to use the standard EQ and keep volume at 50% or less to achieve it.
The FlyBuds C3 have been a bit of a mixed bag so far, but how do they fare when it comes to sound quality?
Let’s make a few things clear, though. These earbuds aren’t going to provide a wide, nuanced soundstage, impeccable detailing, or expert instrument separation. They can’t provide the quality that a pair of wired earbuds in this price-range, like the Sennheiser CX 80U can open up, for example, and keep things pretty basic. But you know what, they actually get those basics pretty spot on.
They definitely emphasize the bass first, but this works to good effect. When tuning into Right Before My Eyes by N'n'G, the pounding low end hit with impressive depth and agility, without sounding muddy or unregimented. Vocals in the midrange weren’t particularly open or detailed, but they were relatively clear, and drums in the treble was articulate and snappy.
When listening to the 2020 remaster of Giant Steps by John Coltrane, I felt that instruments in the midrange sounded a touch recessed, but by giving them a bump with some EQ tweaks, they sounded clean and fairly expressive, and the keys were well-separated from the leading sax.
Overall, the FlyBuds C3 provide good sound for their price. Treble can get a little edgy at the higher volumes, and the mid-range needs a bit of tweaking to sound its best, but the powerful bass really shines here.
In terms of design, the FlyBuds C3 keep it pretty simple, and that’s no bad thing. The earbuds themselves are small and lightweight, and are housed in a curved, ultra-compact charging case, making them perfect for sliding into your pocket. While the buds do have a plasticky and cheap-looking appearance, this can be forgiven for the price, and they do look curved and fairly stylish in-use, whether you go for the black or white color variant.
You also get small, medium, and large ear tips in the box, enabling you to find the perfect fit. For me, the medium ear tips were spot on, and I found the C3 to be very comfortable in use, with no signs of fatigue after a full day’s use. IP55 waterproofing also makes these safe to use when working out or listening in light rain.
The Tribit FlyBuds C3 sound pretty solid for the price, offer decent comfort, and have pretty generous EQ options. However, the models I’ve added in the ‘also consider’ section — the Nothing Ear (a) and JLab Go Pods ANC — deliver better ANC while still offering good sound quality. So, if you can get one of those models at a similar price to the C3, you might get better bang for your buck.
Tribit FlyBuds C3 review: price & release date
- Priced at $39.99 / £49.99 (about AU$60)
- Released in September 2026
The Tribit FlyBuds C3 were released in September 2026, about five years after their predecessor, the FlyBuds C2 hit the market. The C3 deviate from the C2 pretty drastically, offering a proper in-ear seal, as well as active noise cancellation capabilities.
With a list price of $39.99 / £49.99 (about AU$60), the Tribit FlyBuds C3 sit firmly in the budget category. Rivals include the CMF Buds Pro 2, the Earfun Air 2, and the Sony WF-C510.
Tribit FlyBuds C3 review: specs
| Drivers | 10mm dynamic | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | 
| Battery life | 5 hours (buds with ANC on); 8 hours (buds, with ANC off); up to 35 hours (with charging case) | 
| Weight | 4g (per bud) | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Frequency range | 20Hz-20kHz | 
| Waterproofing | IP55 | 
Should I buy the Tribit FlyBuds C3?
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | Great EQ options and solid call quality, but ANC and battery life underwhelm. | 3/5 | 
| Sound quality | Clear sound with deep bass, but not the most detailed and mids need tweaking. | 3.5/5 | 
| Design | A bit plasticky, but very compact and comfortable. | 4/5 | 
| Value | Cheap asking price with good overall quality, but some rivals offer more in terms of ANC. | 4/5 | 
Buy them if…
You want good sound at a low price
The Tribit FlyBuds C3 offer pretty good audio quality, with particularly impressive bass and articulate treble. With some tuning, they also offer pretty expressive sound in the mid-range, making them a very solid, affordable pick.
You want super-comfortable earbuds
I found the C3 to be very comfortable in use, and they come with multiple-sized eartips, helping you to get the perfect fit for long listening sessions.
Don’t buy them if…
You want great ANC
The ANC on the C3 is below average in my opinion, so if you want better noise-cancelling capabilities check out my recommendations in the ‘also consider’ section.
You’re looking for long-lasting battery life
The battery life on the FlyBuds C3 isn’t awful, but it’s certainly nothing special. Five hours per bud with ANC on is pretty unremarkable. The affordable CMF Buds 2 will give you 6.5 hours of battery life with ANC on, which is a considerable step up.
Tribit FlyBuds C3 review: also consider
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Tribit FlyBuds C3 | JLab Go Pods ANC | Nothing Ear (a) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $39.99 / £49.99 (about AU$60) | $36.99 / £29.99 / AU$69.95 | $99 / £99 (about AU$140) | 
| Drivers | 10mm dynamic | 10mm dynamic | 11mm custom | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Battery life | 5 hours (buds with ANC on); 8 hours (buds with ANC off); up to 35 hours (with charging case) | 7.5 hours (buds); 26 hours (with charging case) | 5.5 hours (buds with ANC on); 9.5 hours (buds with ANC off); up to 42.5 hours with charging case) | 
| Weight | 4g (per bud) | 4.2g (per bud) | 4.8g (per bud) | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0 | Bluetooth 5.4 | Row 5 - Cell 3 | 
| Frequency range | 20Hz-20kHz | 20Hz-20kHz | 20Hz-20kHz | 
| Waterproofing | IP55 | IP55 | IP54 | 
JLab Go Pods ANC
The JLab Go Pods ANC are an exceptional value for money option, with solid ANC, a delightfully comfortable in-ear fit, and strong sound quality, marked by regimented bass and well-defined highs. Their battery life isn’t the best (that 7.5 hours figure is with ANC switched off), and they’re not the prettiest buds around, but all in all, we’re still big fans. Read our full JLab Go Pods ANC review.
Nothing Ear (a)
These buds may be a little old now, but as a result, you can often find them on sale for a relatively similar price to the FlyBuds C3. We love the Nothing Ear (a) for their spectacular sound quality, impressive ANC, and stylish looks, so why not give them a go? Read our full Nothing Ear (a) review.
How I tested the Tribit FlyBuds C3
- Spent two weeks testing
- Mainly streamed tracks using Tidal
- Used in the office and when out on walks
I spent two weeks testing the Tribit FlyBuds C3, taking them everywhere with me — to the office, on public transport, and on walks. Testing them out in a variety of environments helped me assess their ANC in full, as well as their transparency mode.
When listening to music, I mainly used the Tidal app on my Xiaomi 17 phone, but I also dipped into Spotify from time to time. As always, I commenced testing by sifting through the TechRadar reference playlist, which features tracks from a variety of genres, but I also listened to hours worth of tunes from my personal library.
More generally, I’ve spent years testing audio gear here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. I’ve tested all sorts of products, from wireless headphones like the Sonos Ace Ultra to Dolby Atmos sounders like the Marshall Heston 120, as well as a huge array of earbuds, including the wired Sennheiser IE 200 and wireless JBL Live Beam 4.
- Read TechRadar’s reviews guarantee
- First reviewed: November 2026
Harry is a Senior Reviews Writer for TechRadar. He reviews everything from party speakers to wall chargers and has a particular interest in the worlds of audio and gaming. Harry has a background in business tech journalism, particularly around the telecoms industry.
